sources.summary: Hayward Gallery, London The photographer finds echoes of Caravaggio and Greek myth in her erotic images, while her disturbing animal montages show that while humans can be beautiful, we are far from innocent It’s the dirty realism of Nan Goldin ’s images, her unfazed photography of the rough seams of spontaneous, dangerous lives, that enables her to create a film of such unlikely ambition as Stendhal Syndrome. This ecstatic condition is named after the French novelist who in 1817 fell ill in Florence, after gorging on the beauty of the Renaissance city’s treasures until “I had palpitations of the heart … I walked with the fear of falling”. Goldin, too, has suffered a bout of this aesthetic delirium, not in Italy but Paris – “the first time I was alone in the Louvre”, she explains on screen. She infects you with it in a ravishing work housed in what looks like a bronze yurt entered via a vaulted corridor. If this seems ostentatious, the film justifies the ceremony. A montage of sensual images teems with Goldin’s uniquely raw, immediate feel for the human presence as she photographs her friends, mostly in the nude, legs wrapped round each other, or lying in a swoon, or touching themselves, or bathing together. Here is the unfeigned, honest impact her work has had since she first put her world viscerally on camera in her early photo series The Ballad of Sexual Dependency . But there’s a difference. items.context: 中央研究院人文社會科學研究中心的研究發現，人生重大負面事件，對幸福感的影響不太一樣。遭遇父母非預期過世的人，快樂程度下降後，大約需要4年才能恢復到原來的水準。但如果是自己或父母健康變差，幸福感下降後就回不去了。跟伴侶分開的人，幸福感的最低點，反而是出現在分開之前。
